thread.title: Students excel again on state tests
thread.title_full: Students excel again on state tests

author: ohtadmin
title: Students excel again on state tests
text:
The proficiency of students in Jamestown is more than double the statewide average in English and math for the sixth consecutive year, according to the 2025 Rhode Island Comprehensive Assessment System.
“I am not surprised at all,” said the superintendent of schools, David Raleigh. “Our students, teachers and staff work hard every day, with strong support from our families. These results reflect that shared commitment and pride. I couldn’t be prouder of both schools.”
Scores from the assessment tests, which were launched during the 2017-18 academic year, were released Oct. 2. The assessment, which tests children in grades 3-8, is broken into four categories: not meeting expectations, partially meeting expectations, meeting expectations and exceeding expectations. Students in the latter two categories are considered proficient.
In English, 193 of the 276 (70 percent) students tested in Jamestown were proficient compared to the statewide average of 33.7 percent. About 15.6 percent of local students exceeded expectations, which is more than three times the statewide average (4.7). Only 4.3 percent of local students did not meet expectations compared to 24.3 percent statewide.
Broken down by school, 67.4 percent of students at Lawn were proficient in English along with 75 percent of Melrose students. Students exceeding expectations were 16 percent and 14.6 percent, respectively, while 6.4 percent of students at Lawn were not meeting expectations.
Not a single student at Melrose was not at least partially meeting expectations in English; all 88 students tested scored in the top three categories.
Only Barrington has a lower percentage of students not meeting expectations in English than Jamestown, and only Barrington and Tiverton have higher percentages of students exceeding them.
The only district with a better overall proficiency rate than Jamestown is Little Compton (76.4).
In math, 189 of the 276 (68.5 percent) students tested in Jamestown were proficient in math with nine students (3.3 percent) not meeting expectations and 36 (13 percent) exceeding them.
Broken down by school, 65.2 percent of Lawn students were proficient at math with 3.2 percent not meeting expectations and 9.5 percent exceeding them.
At Melrose, 75 percent of students were proficient with 3.4 percent not meeting expectations. One in every five students at the elementary school were exceeding expectations.
Jamestown’s rate of 3.3 percent of students not meeting expectations in math is the lowest in the state. Only Little Compton has a better overall proficient rate (72.1 percent) and more students exceeding expectations (16.4 percent).
Eighth-graders at Lawn, who are now freshmen in high school, also were assessed using the Next Generation Science Standards.
Of the 85 students tested, 60 percent (51) were proficient with seven students (8.2 percent) not meeting expectations while 20 (23.5 percent) exceeded them. The statewide averages were 30.8 percent, 22.2 percent and 13.3 percent, respectively.
Jamestown’s proficiency rate in science was bested by five districts with Little Compton at the top (69.2 percent).
Jenn Kittredge, who serves as the district’s instructional coach, said Jamestown’s scores are better than the pre-pandemic grades.
“Since 2019, we’ve adopted strong curricula in these academic areas and our teachers are thoughtful and dedicated to implementing these curricula with integrity,” she said. “In my mind, this means the curricula serves as the guide/road map, but teachers still make the key instructional decisions and undertake the daily shifts and pivots needed to meet each Jamestown student where they are. I can’t say enough about our teachers’ dedication, professionalism and constant willingness to grow their practices no matter the subject or grade level they teach.”
A presentation on the test results will be presented to the school committee at 6 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 23, at Town Hall.
“We’re looking closely at the scores and involving our teachers through small group data discussions to dig deeper into the results,” said Lawn principal Nate Edmunds and Melrose principal Beth Roman in a joint statement. “We’re examining subgroups, grade levels and trends to best understand where we can continue to grow. We’re definitely proud of our students and the teaching and learning that happen each day.”
